readings.c1s1:
¶
'''thereat''' (ᴛ̵ʜãr-at′), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''therat, thereate''; < ''there'' + ''at.''] 1. At that place.

{{smaller block|Wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in ''thereat.''
{{right|Mat. vii. 13.}}}}

2. At that time; upon that.

{{smaller block|''Thereat'' once more he moved about.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Passing of Arthur.}}}}

3. At that thing or doing; on that account.

{{smaller block|Every error is a stain to the beauty of nature; for which cause it blusheth ''thereat.'' {{right|''Hooker.''}}
Bending his sword
To his great master; who, ''thereat'' enraged,
Flew on him.
{{right|''Shak.'', Lear, iv. 2. 75.}}}}

'''thereaway''' (ᴛ̵ʜãr′a̤-wā″), ''adv.'' [< ''there'' + ''away.''] 1. From that place or direction; thence.

{{smaller block|D'ye think we dinna ken the road to England as weel as our fathers before us? All evil comes out o' ''thereaway.''
{{right|''Scott'', Black Dwarf, viii.}}}}

2. In those parts; there; thereabout. [Colloq.]

{{smaller block|There be few wars ''thereaway'' wherein is not a great number of them [Zapolets] in both parties.
{{right|''Sir T. More'', Utopia (tr. by Robinson), ii. 10.}}}}

'''therebefore''' (ᴛ̵ʜãr′bẹ̄-fōr′), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''therbifoore, therbifore, therbeforne''; < ''there'' + ''before.''] Before that time; previously.

{{smaller block|To hym gaf I al the lond and fee,
That ever was me geven ''therbifoore.''
{{right|''Chaucer'', Prol. to Wife of Bath's Tale, l. 631.}}}}

'''thereby''' (ᴛ̵ʜãr-bī′), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''therby, therbi'' (= OFries. ''therbi'' = D. ''daarbij'' = MLG. ''darbi'' = G. ''dabei''); < ''there'' + ''by''<sup>1</sup>.] 1. By that; by that means; in consequence of that.

a consequence from what immediately precedes; they are all affected by their derivation or original meaning. ''Therefore'', for this or that reason, on that account; ''wherefore'', for which reason, on which account. ''Therefore'' is the most formal of the words, and is consequently most used in mathematics, logic, and elaborate argument. The use of ''wherefore'' for ''therefore'' is not to be commended, as it is considered a Latinism to use a relative pronoun or its derivative for a demonstrative or its derivative in carrying on a thought; the development of this principle is modern, and gives to the demonstrative use of ''wherefore'' a tone of quaintness. ''Accordingly'' and ''consequently'' are more common in essay and narrative writing; ''then'' and ''so'' in conversation, where brevity is most studied. The last four are more used to indicate practical sequences.

'''therefro†''' (ᴛ̵ʜãr-frō′), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''therefro''; < ''there'' + ''fro.''] From that.

{{smaller block|And hudden [hid] here egges whan thei ''there-fro'' wente,
For fere of other foules. {{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), xi. 345.}}}}

'''therefrom''' (ᴛ̵ʜãr-from′), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''therfram, tharfrom''; < ''there'' + ''from.''] From that.

{{smaller block|Analytical reasoning is a base and mechanical process, which takes to pieces and examines, bit by bit, the rude material of knowledge, and extracts ''therefrom'' a few hard and obstinate things called facts.
{{right|''T. L. Peacock'', Nightmare Abbey, vi.}}}}

'''theregain†''', ''adv.'' [ME. ''thergeyn, thorgen, therien''; < ''there'' + ''gain''<sup>3</sup>. Cf. ''thereagain.''] Thereagainst.

{{smaller block|If men wolde ''thergeyn'' appose
The nakid text and lete the glose.
{{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 6555.}}}}

'''theregates†''', ''adv.'' [ME. ''ther-gatis''; < ''there'' + ''gate''<sup>2</sup> + adv. gen. ''-es.''] In that way.

{{smaller block|A seede that vs sall saue,
That nowe in blisse are bente.
Of clerkis who-so will craue,}}

¶
'''therese''' (tē-rēs′), ''n.'' [So called from ''Maria Theresa'' (?).] A kerchief or veil of semi-transparent material, worn by women at the close of the eighteenth century.

'''therethence†''' (ᴛ̵ʜãr-thens′), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''ther-thens''; < ''there'' + ''thence''.] Thence; from that.

{{smaller block|He ''ther-thens'' wende towarde Norbelande.
{{right|''Rom. of Partenay'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 3350.}}}}

'''therethorough†''' (ᴛ̵ʜãr-thur′ō), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''therthorw, thærthurh, tharthurh''; < ''there'' + ''thorough''.] Same as ''therethrough''.

{{smaller block|Sorwe to fele,
To wite ''ther-thorw'' what wele was.
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), xxi. 231.}}}}

'''therethrough''' (ᴛ̵ʜãr-thrö′), ''adv.'' [A later form of ''therethorough''. Cf. ''through''<sup>1</sup>, ''thorough''.] Through that; by that means.

{{smaller block|Ye maun be minded not to act altogether on your ain judgment, for ''therethrough'' comes sair mistakes.
{{right|''Scott'', Heart of Mid-Lothian, xliii.}}}}

{{smaller block|Blowing air ''therethrough'' until the carbon is ignited.
{{right|''The Engineer'', LXXI. 42.}}}}

'''theretill†''' (ᴛ̵ʜãr-til′), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''thertil, thertille, thortil'' (= Sw. ''dertill'' = Dan. ''dertil''); < ''there'' + ''till''<sup>2</sup>.] Thereto.

{{smaller block|It was hard for to come ''thertille''.
{{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 3482.}}}}

'''thereto''' (ᴛ̵ʜãr-tö′), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''therto, tharto'' (= OS. ''tharto'' = OFries. ''therto, derto'' = D. ''daartoe'' = OHG. ''darazuo, tharazuo'', MHG. ''darzuo'', G. ''dazu''); < ''there'' + ''to''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' To that.

{{smaller block|As the euangelist wytnesseth whan we maken festes,
We sholde nat clypie [invite] kynghtes ''ther-to'' ne no kyne ryche.
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), xiii. 102.}}}}
readings.c2s3:
¶
2. Also; over and above; to boot.

{{smaller block|A water . . . so depe and brode and ''ther-to'' blakke.
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), ii. 350.}}}}

{{smaller block|I would have paid her kiss for kiss,
With usury ''thereto.'' {{right|''Tennyson'', Talking Oak.}}}}

'''theretofore''' (ᴛ̵ʜãr′tö-fōr′), ''adv.'' [< ''thereto'' + ''fore.''] Before that time: the counterpart of ''heretofore.'' [Rare.]

{{smaller block|They sought to give to the office the power ''theretofore'' held by a class.
{{right|''N. A. Rev.'', CXLIII. 238.}}}}

'''thereunder''' (ᴛ̵ʜãr-un′dėr), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''therunder, thorunder'' (= OS. ''tharundar'' = OFries. ''therunder'' = D. ''daaronder'' = MHG. ''drunder'', G. ''darunter'' = Sw. Dan. ''derunder''); < ''there'' + ''under.''] Under that.

{{smaller block|Those which come nearer unto reason find Paradise under the equinoctial line; . . . judging that ''thereunder'' might be found most pleasure and the greatest fertility.
{{right|''Raleigh'', Hist. World, I. iii. § 7.}}}}

'''thereunto''' (ᴛ̵ʜãr-un′tö), ''adv.'' [< ''there'' + ''unto.''] Thereto.

{{smaller block|Either St. Paul did only by art and natural industry cause his own speech to be credited; or else God by miracle did authorize it, and so bring credit ''thereunto.''
{{right|''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity, iii. 8.}}}}

'''thereup†''', ''adv.'' [ME. ''theruppe, theroppe, thruppe''; < ''there'' + ''up.''] Same as ''thereupon.''

'''thereupon''' (ᴛ̵ʜãr″u-pon′), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''therupon, theruppon''; < ''there'' + ''upon.''] 1. Upon that.
